performers: The Tudor Consort; Michael Stewart, director
question: How does overlapping vocal writing keep the music moving through a cadence?
intro: The Tudor Consort sings the motet rather than the Mass which shares its title. Listen for the way separate vocal lines keep a phrase moving when another part reaches a resting point.

sections.label: Opening imitations
sections.mNote: the opening point passes successively through the five parts

sections.label: Central phrases
sections.mNote: new text phrases overlap the ends of earlier ones

sections.label: Closing span
sections.mNote: the concluding acclamation extends the imitative texture

cues.title: Five lines, one motet
cues.text: Palestrina writes five vocal parts: cantus, altus, tenor, a second tenor and bassus. Their entries accumulate rather than presenting the whole ensemble as a single block; follow a melodic shape as it passes from one line to another.
cues.evidence: The 1862 collected score, No. 21, begins on printed p. 90 and names all five parts; the opening entries are staggered. No entry after the opening is assigned a precise second. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f5/IMSLP55722-PMLP115176-Tomus_I.pdf

cues.title: The first motet collection
cues.text: This five-voice setting appears in Palestrina’s first collection of motets, published in Rome in 1569. Publication gives a firm point in its history; the date at which he composed it is not established here.
cues.evidence: IMSLP identifies the 1569 Motettorum, Liber 1 and lists Sicut lilium as No. 21; John Milsom’s programme note independently identifies this five-voice setting and publication. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15060_GBLLH1645012

cues.title: A cadence does not stop everyone
cues.text: Across these interwoven phrases, listen below the upper line. A lower voice may continue while another rests or holds its last note. The distinction between a local resting point and a complete stop keeps the motet moving.
cues.evidence: Printed pp. 90–92 show different phrase lengths, held notes and rests among the parts. This is a general listening invitation, not identification of an individual lower-voice entry at 1:10.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A biblical love comparison
cues.text: The text comes from the Song of Songs: a beloved is compared with a lily among thorns. Palestrina’s setting expands this short comparison through repeated words and overlapping voices, rather than adding a narrative with new events.
cues.evidence: Milsom identifies the biblical source and paraphrases the comparison; the score sets Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias Adae, followed by Alleluia. This note is contextual, not a timestamped transcription.

cues.title: Follow one inner part
cues.text: Choose an inner line for a few phrases rather than following only the highest voice. Its sustained notes can become dissonant as the other parts move, then settle by step; the harmony is the result of several independent motions.
cues.evidence: The viewed five-part score, especially printed pp. 91–93, supplies the independent motion and held-note dissonances. No machine chord label, exact suspension or bar number is assigned to this cue.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A motet becomes a Mass
cues.text: Palestrina later makes this motet the model for a Mass with the same title. The opening imitative point is carried into the Kyrie. This recording is the short motet itself, not one of that Mass’s movements.
cues.evidence: Peter Phillips’s note identifies the Mass’s borrowing of the motet’s opening point. The FMA album lists the motet first and the separate Mass movements afterwards. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W15061_810202

cues.title: A retreat before renewed weight
cues.text: A stronger stretch gives way to a brief reduction in recorded sound, then the ensemble builds again. Keep following the continuing vocal lines across that retreat instead of treating it as the end of the motet.
cues.evidence: The report places its loudest window around 3:25, a substantial drop by 3:35, and renewed level at 3:40–3:45. The boundary at 3:34 anchors this broad contrast, not a particular sung word.

cues.title: The last sustained span
cues.text: The closing stretch rises again before the sound withdraws. Listen for the difference between the voices settling on their final sonority and the room’s remaining resonance.
cues.evidence: High-level windows around 4:05–4:15 precede a reduction at 4:20 and a final fall from 4:30 to 4:35. The score closes in sustained notes, but the release is not aligned to a specific second.

transitions.title: An ending overlaps the next phrase
transitions.how: The opening point gives way to fresh text phrases without a general pause. Palestrina lets one voice hold its closing note while another begins the next idea; the five-part texture changes its internal balance rather than replacing the choir with a new sound. The overlap makes the cadence a hinge within the motet, not a final full stop.
transitions.evidence: The score’s move from the opening words to sic amica mea is visible on printed p. 91, with held notes and overlapping entries. The quieter 1:25–1:30 region and measured boundary at 1:36 support a broad central grouping. The actual first syllable is not aligned.

transitions.title: The final acclamation grows from overlapping lines
transitions.how: The concluding Alleluia is not set apart by a new ensemble. Its entries overlap the close of the preceding phrase and then extend the same imitative method towards the final sustained sonority. Listen through the temporary reduction in sound: the ending is built by renewed participation within the choir rather than by an instrumental addition.
transitions.evidence: Printed pp. 93–94 show the overlap into Alleluia and the ensuing imitative close. The report’s strong boundary at 3:34 and level recovery after 3:35 support the approximate closing span; no word or individual entry is timed.

source.title: Palestrina, Motettorum, Liber 1, No. 21, ed. Theodor de Witt (1862)
source.locator: Printed pp. 90–94 (PDF pp. 104–108). Cantus, altus, tenor, quintus (second tenor), bassus. Ensemble-level scoring only; the choir’s edition and individual entry times are unestablished.
